aliases: Tong Tian Xiang Jiang Hua Xiang
cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Jiang Hua Xiang strain (Tong Tian Xiang mother-tree lineage)
processing: Classic Wudong dancong processing: sun-withering, firm overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, strip rolling and a light-to-medium charcoal roast in two or three passes with rests between them; mother-tree and close-cutting lots are processed in tiny separate batches.
harvest_season: One spring picking in late April or early May on Wudong; the mother tree is picked over a day or two and processed alone, its cuttings in small batches.
appearance_dry: Long, heavy, dark brown strips with an intense spicy-floral smell.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, leathery olive leaves with red edges.
taste_profile: Ginger-lily spice and honey at full volume, a thick, oily body with ripe fruit, and a mountain-rhyme mineral finish that cools the throat for minutes.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps, soft water. Drink it on its own, not after a perfumed tea, and keep going past the sixth steep: the aftertaste is the reason for the price.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year with the garden or tree named, released in autumn after two or three roasts and rests, and often held a year before sale; it keeps three to five years sealed and dry and is one of the dancongs sold aged with the vintage stated. Tea from the mother tree itself is allocated in tiny amounts; what reaches shops comes from cuttings at various distances from it.
description:
Tong Tian Xiang, the fragrance that reaches heaven, is the name of one tree and of the tea descended from it: the famous old ginger-flower (Jiang Hua Xiang) dancong in the hamlet of Zhong Ping on Wudong, the highest tea village of the Fenghuang Mountains. It is the most celebrated single mother tree in Chaozhou after the Song Zhong, and its cuttings make a spicy, honeyed, deeply mineral dancong.

The tree is traditionally said to be several hundred years old, and the name comes from the local claim that its scent carried far enough to reach the sky when the leaves were being processed. What is not in doubt is that it is the source of the Jiang Hua Xiang aroma type: the ginger-lily strain grown across the range comes from cuttings taken from it, and tea sold as Tong Tian Xiang is tea from the tree or from its closest descendants on Wudong, while Jiang Hua Xiang is the same strain grown anywhere.

The making is the patient Wudong method: a firm overnight shaking to a medium oxidation, which brings out the spice, strip rolling and a light-to-medium charcoal roast done in two or three passes over the summer with rests in between. Old-tree leaf is thick and takes that roasting without losing aroma, and it gains the dried-fruit and woody depth that Chaozhou drinkers prize.

In the cup it is Jiang Hua Xiang with the volume up and the floor dropped out: ginger-lily and white-flower spice, honey, ripe fruit, a thick oily texture, and a long, cold mineral aftertaste called shan yun. It runs ten steeps or more and improves as the session goes on; brew it hot, fast and with soft water, and never after a loud tea.

It is sold by year, usually in autumn or the following year, with the tree or garden named, and the real thing exists in kilograms. The name is borrowed freely for ordinary Jiang Hua Xiang, so buy from an established Chaozhou seller, start with a small sample, and compare it with their high-mountain Jiang Hua Xiang: if the difference in depth and length is not obvious, you are paying for the story.
sources_note: Tree age and the name story are traditional. Some sellers use Tong Tian Xiang and Jiang Hua Xiang interchangeably; here Tong Tian Xiang is treated as the mother-tree lineage and Jiang Hua Xiang as the aroma type, which is the usual Chaozhou distinction.
